claims.text: The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy is in a conventional cast or homogenized, relatively coarse-grained state.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 786 MPa yield strength.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 1314 MPa compressive strength.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a 13.5% terminal strain under tensile testing.
Cold rolling followed by controlled recrystallization annealing will produce a fine, homogeneous, equiaxed grain structure in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The refined microstructure will improve uniform strain distribution and tensile ductility.
The refined microstructure will enhance dislocation mobility.
Thermo-mechanical processing will preserve lattice-distortion effects arising from the refractory elements.
Additional grain boundaries will inhibit dislocation pile-up and delay strain localization.
Intrinsic lattice distortion contributes to the high strength of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Preserving lattice distortion will preserve impact-triggered energy release.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation from 13.5% to approximately 20% or higher.
The treatment will limit the reduction in yield strength to less than 10% relative to approximately 786 MPa.
The treatment will limit the reduction in compressive strength to less than 10% relative to approximately 1314 MPa.
Impact energy release after treatment will remain similar to the untreated baseline.
The hypothesis is restricted to room-temperature tensile loading at an approximately 10^-3 s^-1 quasi-static strain rate.
Excessive grain coarsening during annealing would undermine the proposed treatment.
Performance at elevated temperatures or higher strain rates remains untested and uncertain.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% baseline is identified as terminal strain, but the prediction treats it as the baseline uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct measurements and cannot be interchanged without justification.

The conditions associate quasi-static loading specifically with tensile testing, whereas the experimental design says tensile, compression, and impact tests will all be conducted under quasi-static conditions. An impact test is intrinsically dynamic, so its loading-rate specification is incoherent.
